entry.title: FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

link.title: FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

entry.content:
This blog post summarizes our paper, FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction, which builds on our prior work, HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method.

TL;DR: We introduce a framework that generates hypergraphs with node and hyperedge features, based on an “unzoom–zoom” principle. First, the input hypergraph is coarsened into increasingly simplified representations (“unzoom”) by merging nodes and hyperedges. We track how many nodes each cluster represents and average features accordingly. Then, we train a model to reconstruct fine-grained structure from these coarse versions (“zoom”). Generation is performed by repeatedly applying the model to zoom in and increase detail until a full hypergraph is synthesized.

Preliminaries

A random graph and a random hypergraph.

Traditional graphs consist of nodes connected by edges, each linking exactly two nodes. Hypergraphs, by contrast, allow hyperedges to connect any number of nodes, capturing higher-order relationships. This makes hypergraphs especially expressive in domains such as:

  • 3D meshes, where faces can be represented as 3-edges
  • Electronic circuits, with routers modeled as hyperedges connecting all components
  • Molecular structures, where functional groups (e.g., carboxylic acids) can form hyperedges

Our aim is to build a deep learning method that can generate new samples from distributions of featured hypergraphs — for example, to synthesize new 3D shapes resembling input mesh variants. While HYGENE addressed topology generation, FAHNES extends this by improving structural quality and supporting features.

Examples of datasets we tested our method against

In short, given a dataset of featured hypergraphs (with 3D positions, labels, or other features) sharing similar topologies, our goal is to train a model that can generate new, plausible instances.

Main inspirations

FlowAR: Scale-wise Autoregressive Image Generation Meets Flow Matching

FlowAR generates images by upsampling and denoising step by step: each step upsamples the previous image (e.g., from 8×8 to 16×16) and refines it through flow-matching, conditioned on the upsampled version from the previous step.

HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method

Our approach builds on HYGENE, which introduced a multi-scale “unzoom–zoom” scheme:

1. Hypergraph Downsampling (Unzoom)

We coarsen the hypergraph using two graph projections:

  • Clique Expansion: Replaces each hyperedge with a weighted clique, preserving spectral properties and allowing graph coarsening.
  • Star Expansion (Bipartite View): Represents the hypergraph as a bipartite graph with nodes on one side and hyperedges on the other.

We apply a spectral-preserving coarsening algorithm on the clique expansion, and mirror the same merges in the bipartite view. Hyperedges are merged when their node sets become identical.

Coarsening: (a) Clique expansion with edge weights; (b) coarsening with spectral preservation; (c) mirrored merging in the bipartite view.

2. Hypergraph Upsampling (Zoom)

We train a model to reverse the coarsening process:

  • Expansion: Predicts new nodes/hyperedges from coarse ones, maintaining connections.
  • Refinement: Filters edges to enforce structural consistency.

At generation time, we start from a minimal graph and expand it iteratively.

Starting from a minimal bipartite graph, our model expands both node and hyperedge sets while preserving structure and features through refinement.

Our Work

FlowAR excels at generating features but lacks topology modeling. HYGENE, conversely, generates topology but not features. Our method bridges this gap by adding support for node budgets, feature-aware hierarchical generation, and refinement.

Coarsening Sequence / Downsampling

Each node and hyperedge initially has a node budget of one. As nodes are merged during coarsening, the resulting cluster’s budget becomes the sum of its components. Features are averaged using budget-weighted means. Thus, each cluster encodes the average feature of the nodes it represents.

During generation, child nodes/hyperedges inherit the coarse feature and are refined by the model to predict their finer features.

Coarsening sequences on different meshes. Broad lines represent 2-edges.

Coarsening Inversion / Upsampling

Instead of directly predicting child node budgets, the model learns splitting ratios — i.e., what fraction of the parent’s budget each child receives. This constrains outputs to [0, 1] and improves training stability. Inputs are encoded with sinusoidal positional embeddings to reduce variance.

For features, the coarse feature is first duplicated across children (like a pixelated image), and the model refines it — similar to FlowAR’s coarse-to-fine enhancement.

The pipeline: i) Coarsen the hypergraph with feature and budget tracking. ii) Train the model to reverse merges. iii) Generate by expanding and refining structure and features iteratively.

Results and Limitations

Results

Generated samples for the datasets shown earlier.

Limitations

In molecule generation, our model is outperformed by one-shot predictors. We hypothesize this is due to the discrete nature of our generation process. In image generation, small errors yield small differences — nearby pixels stay close in latent space. But in hypergraph generation, small prediction errors (e.g., adding/removing an edge) can alter topology drastically, changing the message-passing structure and disrupting embeddings. One-shot models are more robust because they operate on fixed connectivity.

Conclusion

This work is a step toward hierarchical, feature-aware hypergraph generation. Future work will aim to improve robustness to prediction errors and better model discrete structure.

If you use our work, please cite:

@inproceedings{gailhard2025hygene,
  title={Hygene: A diffusion-based hypergraph generation method},
  author={Gailhard, Dorian and Tartaglione, Enzo and Naviner, Lirida and Giraldo, Jhony H.},
  booktitle={Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence},
  volume={39},
  number={16},
  pages={16682--16690},
  year={2025}
}

entry.title: FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

link.title: FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

entry.content:
This blog post summarizes our paper, FAHNES: Feature-Aware Hypergraph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction, which expands our work HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method.

TL;DR: We introduce a framework able to generate hypergraphs with node and hyperedge features, based on an “unzoom-zoom” principle. First, we compute increasingly coarse versions of a hypergraph (“unzoom”), keeping track of the number of nodes in each supernode/superhyperedge and averaging features. Then, we train a model to reconstruct the original details from these simplified versions (“zoom”). Generation is achieved by repeatedly applying the trained model to zoom in, gradually increasing detail until the desired hypergraph size is reached.

Preliminaries

A random graph and a random hypergraph.

Traditional graphs consist of nodes connected by edges, with each edge linking precisely two nodes. Hypergraphs, however, offer a more versatile framework. In a hypergraph, edges — referred to as hyperedges — can connect an arbitrary number of nodes simultaneously. This generalization allows hypergraphs to capture higher-order and more nuanced relationships compared to standard graphs. This also makes them much more expressive, for instance:

  • 3D meshes can be represented with triangles as 3-edges
  • Electronic circuits can be modeled with routers replaced by hyperedges connecting all associated components
  • Molecules can be depicted more accurately, with functional groups like carboxylic acids joined into hyperedges to highlight their higher-order relationship

Our work aims to develop a deep-learning based method capable of generating new samples from a given distribution of featured hypergraphs. For instance, given examples of 3D meshes representing variants of an object, we want to train a model that can generate new instances. Generating topology was already addressed with HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method, so here we focus on improving the quality of generated topology and adding support for features.

Examples of datasets we tested our method against

In other words, given a dataset of featured hypergraphs (with 3D positions, component types, or other characteristics) that share similar topological properties, our goal is to train a model capable of generating new hypergraphs with matching properties.

Main inspirations

FlowAR: Scale-wise Autoregressive Image Generation Meets Flow Matching

Beginning with a single pixel, at every generation step FlowAR upsample the current image (i.e. replace each pixel by a 2x2 block with the same value) that will serve as conditioning for the next round of flow-matching: starting from a gaussian noise, the model iteratively denoises the image to generate the final output, while conditioned on the upsampled prediction from the previous step.

HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method

Our method for hypergraph generation builds on our previous work HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method, which uses an “unzoom–zoom” scheme:

1. Hypergraph Downsampling (Unzoom)

To enable coarsening on hypergraphs, we project them into graph space using two complementary representations:

  • Clique Expansion: Each hyperedge is replaced with a clique of edges weighted by \(1/ \vert e \vert\), where \(\vert e \vert\) is the hyperedge size. This preserves spectral properties, allowing us to apply traditional coarsening methods.

  • Star Expansion (Bipartite View): The hypergraph is represented as a bipartite graph. One set of nodes corresponds to original hypergraph nodes, the other to hyperedges, with links connecting nodes to the hyperedges they belong to.

We apply a spectrum-preserving coarsening algorithm to the clique expansion to produce a hierarchy of coarsened graphs. The same node merges are mirrored in the bipartite representation, and hyperedges are merged when their node sets become identical (i.e. the same hyperedge appears twice).

Coarsening: (a) Compute the weighted clique expansion by collapsing each hyperedge into an appropriately weighted clique. (b) Coarsen the clique expansion while preserving the spectral properties of the hypergraph (dark blue nodes). (c) Update the bipartite view: corresponding left side nodes (in dark blue) are merged, then right side nodes representing the same hyperedge (circled in black) are merged.

2. Hypergraph Upsampling (Zoom)

From a reduced bipartite graph, we train a neural network to reverse the coarsening process:

  • Expansion: Predicts which nodes and hyperedges should be duplicated at each step. New entities inherit connections from their parent nodes/hyperedges.

  • Refinement: Filters the resulting edges to ensure structural similarity.

For generation, starting with a single node and single hyperedge, we apply this expansion + refinement step iteratively to recover a full-size hypergraph.

Our model starts from a single pair of linked nodes (in the bipartite representation) and iteratively expands the left-side nodes (in dark blue) and right-side nodes (in red), where each duplicate keeps the connections of its parent node. Then, our method refines the resulting bipartite graph filtering edges to recover an appropriate local structure.

Our Work

FlowAR can generate features but is unable to generate topology. On the other hand, HYGENE can generate topology but cannot generate features. Our work combines both to allows generating featured hypergraphs for various modalities. Our contributions are the addition of a node-budget mechanism, representing the size of each cluster (i.e. how many nodes it contains), and the integration of hierarchical generation to our setting.

Coarsening Sequence / Downsampling

During coarsening, every node and hyperedge starts with a node budget of one (coarsening has not started yet, so each “cluster” represents a single node, itself) ; then, for each merging of clusters, the resulting supernode / superhyperedge inherits the sum of the node budgets of the nodes / hyperedges it contains. Node/hyperedge features are averaged when merging several nodes, the weights in the averaging being the node budgets. That way, each cluster has as feature the average of all the nodes it contains. During generation, children of a node / hyperegde obtain the same feature as their parent (“coarse features”), and the model is tasked with predicting the new features (“refined features”).

The following figure depicts such coarsening sequences for various meshes.

Examples of coarsening sequences for various meshes. Broad lines represent 2-edges.

Coarsening Inversion / Upsampling

During inversion of the coarsening, in order to have a constrained space for the predictions of node budgets, the model is not tasked to directly generate the resulting node budgets for all children of a cluster, but rather tasked with predicting the splitting of node budgets. Indeed, during training, we task it to predict the ratio between the ground truth value for the refined node budget and the parent node budget. That way, predictions are constrained in [0, 1], which helps learning as it reduces the variance of target outputs. Additionally, to ensure that input variance is also controlled, we use a sinusoidal positional encoding to transform the integers.

For features, the process is done similarly as for hierarchical image generation. First, the children nodes of a cluster are first given the same feature as their parent (i.e. we have a “pixelated” version of the hypergraph). Then, based on these coarse features, the model enhances and refines the features (i.e. it computes the clear hypergraph from its pixelated version).

The following figure explains our strategy.

Combining everything gives the above pipeline: i) During training, input hypergraphs are progressively _coarsened_ by merging nodes and hyperedges, yielding a multiscale representation. Node features are averaged during merging, and budgets are summed. ii) The model is trained to predict which nodes were merged at each scale. iii) In the _expansion_ phase, merged nodes are expanded (shown in dark), inheriting their parent’s features, budget, and connectivity. The model is trained to (a) identify which edges should be removed (dotted lines), (b) predict how the parent’s budget should be split across the children (instead of predicting absolute values), and (c) refine the features of newly expanded nodes (_refinement_).

Results and Limitations

Results

Examples of generated samples corresponding to the datasets shown at the beginning.

Limitations

Results for molecule generate show that our method is not competitive compared to one-shot graph prediction methods, unlike hierarchical image generation which is stronger than regular one-shot methods. We hypothesize that the difference stems from the discrete nature of the generation process: for continuous predictions with fixed topology (like for images), the “latent space” is “continuous”, in the sense that nodes (i.e. pixels) of slightly different images have slightly different representations. Thus a small error during a prediction step results in a slightly different starting point. This is not true in our discrete setting, due to the tresholding effect of either adding an edge or removing it, expanding a cluster or not: a small error at a prediction step results in a different topology, which changes a lot the underlying embedding (with a GNN, either the information passes or not). One-shot models do not suffer from that, as the topology (a fully connected graph) is fixed during generation.

Conclusion

This work represents a significant first step towards featured hierarchical (hyper)graph generation. Our future research will focus on rendering the framework more robust to perturbations / prediction errors.

When using our work, please cite our paper:

@inproceedings{gailhard2025hygene,
  title={Hygene: A diffusion-based hypergraph generation method},
  author={Gailhard, Dorian and Tartaglione, Enzo and Naviner, Lirida and Giraldo, Jhony H.},
  booktitle={Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence},
  volume={39},
  number={16},
  pages={16682--16690},
  year={2025}
}

Acknowledgments

We acknowledge the ANR – FRANCE (French National Research Agency) for its financial support of the System On Chip Design leveraging Artificial Intelligence (SODA) project under grant ANR-23-IAS3-0004. This project has also been partially funded by the Hi!PARIS Center on Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence.

entry.title: HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method

link.title: HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method

entry.content:
This blog post will summarize our paper, HYGENE: A Diffusion-based Hypergraph Generation Method, accepted at AAAI-25. To the best of our knowledge, this work introduces the first deep-learning based method for hypergraph generation. Code is available here.

TL;DR: We introduce a hypergraph generation method based on an “unzoom-zoom” principle. First, we compute increasingly coarse versions of a hypergraph (“unzoom”). Then, we train a model to reconstruct the original details from these simplified versions (“zoom”). To simplify processing, we project hypergraphs into graph space using two different projections, each preserving specific characteristics. Generation is achieved by repeatedly applying the trained model to zoom in, gradually increasing detail until the desired hypergraph size is reached.

Preliminaries

A random graph and a random hypergraph.

Traditional graphs consist of nodes connected by edges, with each edge linking precisely two nodes. Hypergraphs, however, offer a more versatile framework. In a hypergraph, edges — referred to as hyperedges — can connect an arbitrary number of nodes simultaneously. This generalization allows hypergraphs to capture higher-order and more nuanced relationships compared to standard graphs. This also makes them much more expressive, for instance:

  • 3D meshes can be represented with triangles as 3-edges
  • Electronic circuits can be modeled with routers replaced by hyperedges connecting all associated components
  • Molecules can be depicted more accurately, with functional groups like carboxylic acids joined into hyperedges to highlight their higher-order relationship
Examples of hypergraph applications

Our work aims to develop a deep-learning based method capable of generating new samples from a given distribution of hypergraphs. For instance, given examples of 3D meshes representing variants of an object, we want to train a model that can generate new instances. As an initial step, we focus solely on the underlying topology of hypergraphs, disregarding features of nodes and hyperedges.

Examples of datasets we tested our method against

In other words, given a dataset of unfeatured hypergraphs (without 3D positions, component types, or other characteristics) that share similar topological properties, our goal is to train a model capable of generating new hypergraphs with matching properties.

Main Inspiration

Our work builds upon the foundation laid by the paper Efficient and Scalable Graph Generation through Iterative Local Expansion, which introduces an innovative method for graph generation. This approach draws inspiration from the tradition of graph coarsening algorithms.

When graphs become excessively large, certain algorithms may become computationally infeasible. To address this, it is possible to create smaller, representative versions of the original graph (called coarsened versions) that retain key characteristics and properties. The authors of the aforementioned paper employed a spectrum-preserving graph coarsening technique. This method merges pairs of adjacent nodes in a way that preserves a subspace of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the original graph, maintaining crucial structural information.

During coarsening, pairs of adjacent nodes are iteratively merged in order to create a reduced version of the graphs while preserving its spectral properties, i.e., preserving its structural information. For instance, the above coarsening sequence preserves the two-blocks structure of the graph and does not merge them until the final step.

The coarsening algorithm is applied iteratively to create a coarsening sequence. The first element in this sequence is the original graph, while the last is a fully reduced version comprising a single node. The challenge then becomes training a model to invert this coarsening process.

Starting from a step in the sequence, the model must identify which nodes result from merging at the previous step. These nodes are then duplicated and connected, with each child retaining the connections of its parent node (expansion). A second model then determines which edges should be retained in the final graph (refinement).

At each step, a first model chooses which nodes need to be duplicated before a second model filters out the resulting edges.

The generation process simply involves applying this expansion and refinement procedure iteratively until obtaining a graph of the desired size. This approach scales more efficiently compared to existing techniques, as it leverages the graph’s sparsity. When two parts of the graph become disconnected during an early generation step, there’s no need to check for connections later, significantly reducing computational overhead.

Our Work

We have successfully generalized this generation method to hypergraphs and tested it on several datasets. Given the challenges of working directly with hypergraphs due to variable hyperedge sizes and complex node relationships, we project the problem back into graph space using two equivalent representations.

Coarsening Sequence / Downsampling

Coarsening: (a) Compute the weighted clique expansion by collapsing each hyperedge into an appropriately weighted clique. (b) Coarsen the clique expansion while preserving the spectral properties of the hypergraph (dark blue nodes).

To apply coarsening algorithms to hypergraphs, we represent them as their clique expansion. In this representation, each hyperedge \(e\) is transformed into a clique weighted by \(1/ \vert e \vert\) , where \(\vert e \vert\) is the size of the hyperedge. When an edge appears in multiple cliques, its weight becomes the sum of the weights from each clique.

This clique expansion is particularly useful for coarsening, as it maintains the same number of nodes as the original hypergraph and shares its spectral properties. Consequently, node mergings that preserve spectral properties in the clique expansion also preserve them in the hypergraph. To construct a coarsening sequence for a given hypergraph, we create an equivalent sequence for its clique expansion and merge the same pairs of nodes.

However, it’s important to note that while deriving the clique expansion from a hypergraph is straightforward, the reverse process is NP-hard, which makes it infeasible to work with the clique expansion during generation.

(c) Update the bipartite view: corresponding left side nodes (in dark blue) are merged, then right side nodes representing the same hyperedge (circled in black) are merged.

To address this limitation, we maintain another parallel representation of the hypergraph: the star expansion. This representation depicts the hypergraph as a bipartite graph, with one set of nodes corresponding to the hypergraph’s nodes and the other representing hyperedges. Each node is connected to the hyperedges containing it.

When nodes are merged in the clique expansion, the same nodes are merged in the star expansion. If two nodes representing hyperedges have identical connections (i.e., represent the same hyperedge), they are also merged after the node mergings in the clique expansion. Beware that in this scheme, a single pair of node mergings can result in the merging of up to three hyperedges.

Coarsening Inversion / Upsampling

Our model starts from a single pair of linked nodes (in the bipartite representation) and iteratively expands the left-side nodes (in dark blue) and right-side nodes (in red), where each duplicate keeps the connections of its parent node. Then, our method refines the resulting bipartite graph filtering edges to recover an appropriate local structure.

Beginning from a coarsening step, we train a model to identify which nodes and hyperedges result from merging at the previous coarsening step. These nodes are then expanded (nodes are duplicated twice, while hyperedges can be duplicated two or three times), with each child retaining its parent’s connections. A second model is then trained to selectively filter out regular edges, reconstructing an accurate topology. Generation starts with a single pair of connected node (the minimal bipartite graph) and iteratively applies the above scheme until obtaining a hypergraph of the desired size. Once it is attained, we can retrieve the generated hypergraph by replacing each node representing a hyperedge with a hyperedge connecting all its neighbors.

Pipeline

Combining everything gives the above pipeline: (a) A coarsening algorithm is applied to the clique expansion and generates a coarsening sequence by merging pairs of adjacent nodes. (b) A bipartite representation is maintained in parallel, where nodes representing the same hyperedge are merged. (c) A model is trained to invert the coarsening by 1. identifying which nodes are the result of a merging at the previous step and 2. filtering out the edges added during the expansion.

Results and Limitations

Results

Examples of generated samples corresponding to the datasets shown at the beginning.

As illustrated above, our method successfully imitates a variety of properties. For a comprehensive analysis of numerical results across various metrics, please refer to our paper.

Limitations

Our method currently appears to disregard the specified number of nodes during generation, instead sampling from the node count distribution of the training data. Additionally, it encounters difficulties when dealing with datasets containing large hypergraphs.

Conclusion

This work represents a significant first step towards deep-learning based hypergraph generation. Our future research will focus on improving the model’s accuracy during generation, particularly concerning node count adherence, and expanding support for feature generation.

When using our work, please cite our paper:

@inproceedings{gailhard2025hygene,
  title={HYGENE: A diffusion-based hypergraph generation method},
  author={Gailhard, Dorian and Tartaglione, Enzo and Naviner, Lirida and Giraldo, Jhony H.},
  booktitle={Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence},
  volume={39},
  number={16},
  pages={16682--16690},
  year={2025}
}
